Raconda russeliana is a clupeiform fish found in coastal waters of the northern Indian Ocean, where it occupies a distinctive ecological niche as a relatively small-bodied planktivore. Field surveys have recorded individuals attaining a maximum total length of 245 millimeters, though the species is typically encountered at considerably smaller sizes in routine trawl samples. This species exhibits a rapid life-history strategy, with fish reaching the onset of sexual maturity at a standard length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], a threshold that correlates with significant shifts in energy allocation from somatic growth to reproductive development. The weight at which this pubertal transition occurs has been estimated at approximately 7.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 7.3 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from specimens collected in the Bay of Bengal. Such a modest body mass at maturity is consistent with patterns observed in other small tropical clupeiforms, which typically prioritize early reproduction over extended somatic accumulation. Comparisons with larger-bodied congeners highlight the relatively compressed growth phase that characterises this species, as individuals channel resources toward reproductive competence at a standard length substantially below the maximum achievable within their lifetime.

The reproductive biology of Raconda russeliana follows a pattern typical of many iteroparous tropical clupeids, with continuous or prolonged spawning seasons that track favourable environmental conditions. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly at the elevated temperatures characteristic of its shallow-water habitat, and experimental observations indicate that eggs incubated at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C] hatch after approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a short incubation period that reduces vulnerability to predation during the most vulnerable pre-hatching phase. The wet weight of newly hatched larvae is remarkably low, with neonates weighing roughly 0.00027 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00027 grams], a value that reflects the small diameter of the yolk-laden egg, which measures 0.866 millimeters across. This minuscule birth mass necessitates an immediate and efficient transition to exogenous feeding before endogenous yolk reserves are exhausted, placing strong selective pressure on larval feeding structures. First feeding typically occurs within hours of chorion rupture, as the yolk-sac larva begins pursuing suitable microzooplankton prey. The rapid depletion of an already modest yolk supply means that any delay in prey detection rapidly becomes lethal, a constraint that likely shapes spawning phenology in this species.

As development proceeds, Raconda russeliana undergoes a period of rapid mass gain that carries individuals from the nanogram-scale hatching weight toward the dimensions characteristic of reproductively active adults. Growth curves fitted to otolith-based age estimates indicate that the ultimate wet weight attained by this species in local populations is approximately 34 grams [Wwi = approximately 34 grams], a ceiling that appears to be determined more by environmental carrying capacity than by intrinsic physiological limits. This asymptotic mass value is notably lower than that predicted by simple length-weight power functions applied to the maximum recorded standard length, suggesting that individuals achieving near-maximal lengths do not always realise the correspondingly high body masses. Field records show that reproductively active females in good condition commonly weigh between 25 and 34 grams, while spent individuals may fall considerably below this range. The length-weight relationship itself follows a positive allometric trajectory typical of clupeiforms, with condition indices fluctuating seasonally in response to plankton bloom dynamics and spawning-related energetic outlays. These patterns underscore the importance of local food availability in shaping adult body size.

The cumulative effect of this accelerated early development is a relatively compressed generation time that enables populations to respond rapidly to favourable environmental shifts. Adults of both sexes are capable of spawning multiple times across an extended reproductive season, and the species' iteroparous strategy ensures continuous recruitment under consistent thermal conditions.

An integrated perspective on the life history of Raconda russeliana reveals a species finely tuned to the pulsed productivity of tropical coastal ecosystems. The transition from a juvenile growth-dominated phase to a reproductive phase, marked by a standard length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 7.3 grams [Wwp = 7.3 grams], occurs relatively early in the lifespan of approximately 2,190 days [am = approximately 2,190 days] at 28.8 °C [T = 28.8 °C].
